decisions.reason: The source constructs a MultiMCP wrapper with the profile mcp_servers entries; runtime session establishment is not asserted.
A FastMCP constructor appears in mcp_server_1.py, a distinct tracked server source file.
A separate FastMCP constructor appears in mcp_server_2.py despite sharing the Calculator display name.
mcp_server_3.py has its own FastMCP source constructor with a different server display name.
The pinned Telegram server Python file contains a FastMCP source constructor, not proof the SSE endpoint was reached.
Two different tracked files contain distinct FastMCP constructor sites; matching displayed names alone do not collapse them into one object.
The YAML entry declares a candidate math server configuration, while successful server startup, initialization and runtime connection were not observed.
The application source calls AgentLoop at one branch-specific location; this is a constructor callsite, not a count of deployed agents.
A second source branch calls AgentLoop, but the source does not show two simultaneous runtime sessions.
The AgentLoop class definition alone does not instantiate or deploy a runnable LLM agent.
Two context-dependent constructor callsites cannot establish that both paths ran or that two agents were deployed concurrently.
The first server's @mcp.tool decorator is a source export candidate, not verified exposure or agent invocation.
The second server has its own @mcp.tool source export candidate and separate file identity.
The search server includes an @mcp.tool decorator that marks source-level export intent.
The Telegram server has an @mcp.tool decorator, not proof the SSE server was up or reachable.
The source invokes session.list_tools in a session path, so tool enumeration is dynamic rather than fixed by this source file.
A second session path calls list_tools, without any observed response or proof a server connected.
The tool_map is populated using tool.name as a dictionary key in the stdio path; concrete remote names remain unknown.
The SSE path also populates tool_map dynamically from remote tool.name, not a source-listed fixed catalogue.
The code calls self.mcp.call_tool for a parsed tool name; runtime availability and permission are not established.
An @mcp.tool decorator is a server export declaration, and cannot alone prove any particular client or agent can invoke the tool.
The source calls list_tools at runtime, so it does not enumerate the actual returned remote tool names statically.
The mcp.resource decorator at this line declares an MCP resource endpoint rather than an mcp.tool export.
The same server display label in two different source files is insufficient evidence of the same MCP server instance.
The source calls list_tools but no response payload, installed MCP server version, or successful runtime enumeration was witnessed.
The source awaits initialize, but this is not proof all declared stdio and SSE server sessions successfully connected.
Use of unqualified tool.name as a dictionary key creates possible overwrites, but no actual duplicate names or collision were observed.
The dispatch call is source-visible but runtime callability depends on discovered tools, connected sessions and effective authorization.
